blocks.tested_text:
Neuropsychological evaluations after acquired brain injury (ABI) are often incomplete. This research examined whether or not the use of clustering could recover a reproducible cognitive structure, taking into account both how data were imputed in the case of missing values and how features were constructed.

The historical analysis consists of 17,406 assessments from 7,285 patients using 14 different tests within six domains and ten different imputation methods. Three descriptive bands of overall severity were obtained by using the UMAP+HDBSCAN method. Using a fixed-reference approach across imputations resulted in a mean adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.710. Additionally, there appears to be a small association between cluster groupings and clinical units; however, it does not appear to provide clear added patient-grouped predictive value beyond broad diagnostic grouping. These findings do not establish sharply discrete phenotypes.

The exploratory extension uses each patient's earliest eligible assessment as the basis for cluster analysis, with 5,828 discovery and 1,457 validation patients. It uses preprocessing fitted to the discovery data for clustering in the original data space, robust mixture models fitted to observed data, 20 independently refitted stochastic imputations, 50 patient subsamples and mixed-effects trajectory models.

Two-group k-means was selected in all twenty imputation screens, with a mean pairwise validation ARI of 0.959; three-group k-means had an ARI of 0.935. Changing from robust to equal-domain scaling substantially changed the three-group assignments (ARI 0.243). The groups also differed in test availability. Robust t mixtures improved the fit to observed data but preferred eight components, the upper limit of the search. Among the 2,013 longitudinally eligible patients, multi-class trajectory models produced groups below the specified 5% size threshold.

The evidence supports reproducible groupings of cognitive scores under particular assumptions about representation and imputation. It does not confirm distinct clinical phenotypes or treatment utility. Independent outcome measures and external cohorts are still needed before clinical use. CogDash presents both analysis designs for research, with the analysis code available at https://github.com/zkunos/thesis_project.

Acquired Brain Injury (ABI) consists of traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), strokes, encephalitis and hypoxic-ischemic injuries. The clinical impact is substantial. TBIs result in millions of emergency room visits/hospital admissions each year [Maas et al., 2017; Brazinova et al., 2021]; ABI can also cause long-term disability among adults of working age, including both physical and emotional/behavioral changes and/or cognitive deficits [Corrigan et al., 2010]. A variety of cognitive domains are affected by ABI, including attention, memory, language and executive function, although the pattern varies considerably among patients.

Such variability presents a practical challenge when developing individualized interventions/rehabilitation plans. Patients who sustain identically severe injuries may have very different cognitive profiles on follow-up evaluations post-ABI, while commonly used triage labels (diagnosis or severity bands) combine different cognitive profiles and mask clinically relevant differences between individuals within identified groupings [Saatman et al., 2008].

This dissertation seeks to address this concern empirically. Rather than employing pre-specified clinical taxonomies on the data set, I use unsupervised cluster analysis to identify cognitive subgroups based upon patients' performance on various neuropsychological tests and then assess the clinical relevance of these identified subgroups. Another potential barrier to analyzing clinically-collected data includes missing values. In many cases, clinicians omit portions of neuropsychological test batteries during assessment due to time constraints, fatigue, clinician judgment and/or patient-related factors that limit completion of all test administrations. Therefore, it is anticipated that there will be non-random omissions of certain test items.

Missing value imputation allows incomplete assessments to be retained; nevertheless, each technique has its own assumptions concerning missing values. There is limited documentation on how those assumptions affect subsequent cluster analysis; this dissertation investigates that dependency directly.

Phenotyping is the process of identifying cognitive subgroups using a data-driven approach. It is still to be determined whether these subgroups represent qualitatively different profiles or gradations of overall severity.

This study addresses four research questions:

Research Question RQ1: Does the use of an unsupervised clustering method on the imputed dataset help identify discrete cognitive phenotypes in individuals who have experienced an acquired brain injury?

Research Question RQ2: To what extent does the selection of an imputation strategy affect the identification of emergent phenotypes?

Research Question RQ3: Are there relationships between patient-cluster assignments and clinical unit assignments? Establishing these associations would suggest that cognitive tiers differ in their distribution among the populations served by different units.

Research Question RQ4: Do cognitive groupings exhibit greater consistency or easier interpretability when clustering uses domain-level composites rather than individual test variables?

The ultimate goal is to construct a replicable phenotyping pipeline for routinely collected clinical data. Missingness will be modeled as part of the rehabilitation process itself rather than considered a posteriori nuisance.

In this dissertation, I test four hypotheses.

Hypothesis H1: Using a UMAP/HDBSCAN pipeline, I expect to find at least two stable cognitive clusters for most imputation methods, with at most 30% of points classified as noise and a silhouette score of at least 0.40.

Hypothesis H2: Under the fixed-reference framework in Chapter 3, I expect consistency in group assignments across imputation methods, with a median pairwise ARI greater than 0.50. This would support assignment robustness across those particular imputations. It would not exclude artifacts shared by the feature representation or establish that the groups correspond to clinical phenotypes.

Hypothesis H3: Chi-square tests should show a statistically significant association between cluster membership and clinical unit, with Cramér's V greater than 0.10. Such a result would indicate differences in the populations served by different clinical units.

Hypothesis H4: Domain-based feature aggregation should reduce redundancy while retaining similar separation between groups. This will be assessed using silhouette scores, variance inflation factors and condition numbers.

An exploratory patient-level extension was developed after the historical H1-H4 analyses. It independently refits clustering across imputations and patient subsamples, compares feature scaling and incomplete-data mixture models, and models longitudinal cognitive scores. The methods and results appear in Sections 3.8 and 4.12. This extension does not retrospectively redefine the original hypotheses.

blocks.tested_text: In clinical practice, acquired brain injury (ABI) refers to damage to the brain that occurs after birth and is not attributable to a congenital or degenerative condition [UK Department of Health and Social Care, 2022]. These include both traumatic and non-traumatic insults including traumatic brain injury (TBI); stroke; encephalitis; and hypoxia/ischemia. While each of these conditions has its own unique pathophysiology, they share rehabilitation challenges: cognitive deficits often help determine long-term functioning after the acute injury. The most commonly used method to evaluate the cognitive deficits resulting from these types of injuries is through neuropsychological testing. Neuropsychological assessments typically use standardized batteries to measure various areas of cognitive function. Specifically, this usually includes assessment of one's ability to process visual spatial information, to process language, to perform tasks requiring executive function, to learn new material and remember it over time (learning/memory), and how quickly one can process information. Practical implications exist for each area assessed. For example, difficulty with attention may limit an individual's ability to participate in therapy sessions. Memory problems can limit the effectiveness of developing compensatory strategies. Executive and language difficulties can affect planning, self-advocacy and communication. Visuospatial deficits may impact an individual's independence in navigating the environment. Therefore, a cognitive profile obtained by means of comprehensive neuropsychological testing may be helpful in providing relevant information for rehabilitation planning, medicolegal purposes, and informing return-to-work decisions.

People with moderate to severe TBI can have lasting cognitive difficulties, and recovery need not proceed uniformly. Longitudinal work has examined functioning over periods as long as ten years [Ponsford et al., 2014]. In their review, Rabinowitz and Levin [2014] describe how cognitive outcomes depend on injury-related factors as well as patient characteristics such as age and pre-injury neuropsychiatric status. Injury severity alone therefore does not fully describe an individual's cognitive profile.

Furthermore, additional variability is introduced through assessment methods. Neuropsychologists modify standardized testing batteries using a number of criteria, including referral questions, patient tolerance for testing and clinical judgment. These modifications produce structured missing data in the resulting database. Multivariate analysis should account for this structure instead of simply treating missing values as a minor technical problem.

blocks.tested_text:
Missing data are common in clinical research [Gravesteijn et al., 2021]. Three mechanisms for missingness were defined by [Rubin, 1976]. Missing completely at random (MCAR) means that missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved values. Under missing at random (MAR), missingness may depend on observed values but, conditional on them, does not depend on the missing values. Missing not at random (MNAR) means that missingness still depends on unobserved values after accounting for observed information.

The missingness mechanism affects which statistical techniques can be used. If the data follow an MCAR pattern, listwise deletion is unbiased, although it typically reduces efficiency. Multiple imputation and maximum likelihood estimation can provide valid inference when the MAR assumption holds and the model has been appropriately specified. Models that assume MNAR require sensitivity analysis, because observed data alone cannot establish the assumptions made about unobserved values [Rubin, 1987].

blocks.description: Literature: clinical missingness and imputation assumptions
blocks.tested_text:
The distinction between missingness mechanisms has particular implications for clinical neuropsychology. Consider a patient with severe attentional impairment who lacks the energy to complete an executive-functioning task, or a disoriented patient who is not given a memory test. In both cases, the missing score may be related to the value that would have been observed had the test been completed. MAR is therefore a working assumption, not an established fact. MNAR patterns may coexist with missingness caused by assessment protocols. Although the observed data alone cannot identify the missingness mechanism, auxiliary variables can make MAR more plausible by accounting for clinically relevant information [Little and Rubin, 2019].

The amount of missing data itself is insufficient to establish the risk of bias. Reasons for missingness and observed relationships between measures also affect imputation reliability. Variables selected for use should provide enough observed information for conditional estimation. Subsequent cluster analyses should examine how decisions about imputation affect the structure that is recovered.

Mean imputation replaces every missing value by the average of the observed values for the same variable.

Mean imputation is very fast and non-iterative. It has the disadvantage of reducing both variance and covariances among variables, distorting marginal distributions and decreasing estimated standard errors. As such, it was utilized solely as a reference point or baseline in this work.

KNN is a non-parametric method, so it can capture the local structure of the data more effectively than mean imputation. Although KNN has many advantages as an imputation technique, there are also a number of limitations to consider when choosing KNN. When you use small values of k you run the risk of fitting the noise rather than the signal. Conversely, if you choose very high values of k you have the possibility of smoothing away important patterns. As the size of the dataset grows, so does the time required for computation, which will be a consideration for larger datasets.

MICE (or Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations), imputes each variable based on all other variables, but with each variable being imputed repeatedly over multiple iterations [van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011]. Depending upon the nature of the variable(s), one could specify different forms of the conditional model; e.g., linear models for continuous variables or logistic models for binary variables. MICE can retain multivariate relationships and produce multiple imputations to quantify uncertainty. Some disadvantages include having to define a model for every variable and potential issues related to convergence.

Predictive mean matching selects imputed values from the observed donor values, so they remain within the observed range. Therefore, it avoids impossible values (for example, a negative score on a test that includes floors). A limited donor pool can, however, lead to repeated use of the same observed values.

MissForest is an iterative random-forest imputation method [Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012]. First, for each variable j a forest f_j is trained based upon rows with observed values for j, using the other variables as predictors. Then missing values are updated using the new forest f_j and this process is repeated until changes are small.

Since MissForest is a non-parametric method, MissForest can learn about complex non-linear relationships among variables and it can also deal with continuous and categorical variables. MissForest often performs well on benchmark datasets. Unfortunately, MissForest can be very computationally expensive and it does scale poorly when there are many observations and/or many trees.

Another iterative method is EM (Expectation Maximization) [Dempster et al., 1977] where there is an E-step that calculates the expected sufficient statistics and an M-step that maximizes the log-likelihood function. blocks.tested_text: Imputation methods for clinical research were categorized by [Afkanpour et al., 2024] into four groups. The first category includes traditional methods, such as mean imputation, EM and MICE. The second includes machine learning methods, such as KNN and MissForest. The third contains hybrid methods, represented here by PMM. The fourth is matrix completion, including SoftImpute and NMF. I add a fifth category for the deep learning methods used in this study, specifically DAEs and VAEs. Comparing methods from each of these categories makes it possible to assess whether the recovered cognitive structure remains consistent despite the different assumptions of the imputation methods.

blocks.tested_text:
Clustering is used as a statistical technique in neuropsychological research. One major method for making clinical judgments about a patient's diagnosis or level of disability post-stroke, traumatic brain injury (TBI), or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is through the use of categorical clinical judgment. Cluster analysis has been utilized across various clinical populations (e.g., TBI; MCI). The results of these analyses indicate that statistically determined subgroups of individuals' performance in areas related to cognition do not always align with the clinical diagnosis or severity categories assigned to the same population. As an empirical evidence-based finding, this suggests that clinicians' utilization of classification systems to identify cognitive variability among individuals post-injury does not fully depict the cognitive variability present.

A literature review of data driven approaches to cognitive phenotyping following brain injury was conducted by [García-Rudolph et al., 2021]. Common trends were observed throughout the reviewed articles. Firstly, many studies reported identifying two to four statistically derived cognitive clusters. Secondly, many of these studies identified clusters primarily by determining which cognitive abilities were relatively stronger than weaker compared to an individual's global level of cognitive ability. Lastly, where applicable and relevant, group membership was found to be significantly related to clinically meaningful outcomes (i.e., return to work).

Several gaps remain in the literature on data-driven cognitive phenotyping after brain injury. Many prior studies had sample sizes ranging from about 100 to fewer than 200 participants. Missing values were frequently excluded through complete-case methods. Although this can be appropriate when missingness is completely random (MCAR), it can bias the resulting sample when missingness is informative. Few studies have evaluated the sensitivity of clustering algorithms to different parameters.

This dissertation therefore uses four design elements to address these limitations. Chapter 3 uses a larger clinical database; compares ten imputation methods with one another and with complete-case analysis; evaluates sensitivity to hyperparameters and missingness thresholds; and uses HDBSCAN as an alternative to k-means. Unlike k-means, HDBSCAN does not require the number of clusters k to be chosen in advance. It finds dense regions of observations and can leave isolated points classified as noise rather than forcing them into predetermined centroids.

The UMAP algorithm for dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN for cluster identification represent the core elements of the clustering process.

The first component (the UMAP) applies a form of non-linear manifold learning. This approach provides low dimensional representations of high dimensional data that aim to retain aspects of its original topology. Unlike PCA and other linear reductions, UMAP can represent non-linear relationships in the original data. Since there exists some compromise between preserving the overall shape of the data (global) and capturing the finer detail (local), we have three parameters which can assist us in achieving a suitable level of compromise among these competing requirements:

n_neighbors: A measure of how many neighboring points should be considered when constructing the neighborhood graph in the original space. Larger values result in a broader view of the global characteristics of the data; smaller values allow for greater examination of local relationships.

min_dist: This parameter governs how closely points can sit together in the reduced space. Larger settings spread points out more, whereas smaller settings allow groups to be represented more compactly.

n_components: The target number of dimensions in the new space.

HDBSCAN adds additional features beyond what traditional DBSCAN does with regard to creating hierarchical clustering of the data at various levels of density and determining those elements of the data that are common across multiple clusterings. Traditional DBSCAN has difficulty recovering both variable-density and nested clusters using a single, fixed neighborhood radius. HDBSCAN addresses this through a density hierarchy, selecting stable clusters and labeling other points as noise without requiring a fixed number of clusters. The three key parameters of HDBSCAN are:

min_samples: Density estimation parameter.

min_cluster_size: The smallest acceptable cluster size.

cluster_selection_epsilon: The distance threshold for merging nearby clusters.

Beyond modifying distance measurements according to local density, HDBSCAN uses mutual reachability (defined in Equation 2.15) to connect observations. A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), built upon these modified distances, forms the foundation for a hierarchical representation. The resulting hierarchy represents individual observations and their successive groupings. Then, persistent clusters are chosen based on stability; as described in Equation 2.16, where λ_birth(C) represents the density level at which cluster C was created, and λ_max(x,C) represents the highest density level at which x belonged to cluster C. All remaining objects not assigned to a persistent cluster are identified as noise.

blocks.tested_text: Internal validation considers different aspects of cluster solutions. This study primarily uses silhouette coefficients [Rousseeuw, 1987] to compare cohesion within a cluster with separation from the nearest alternative cluster, using distances between observations. An individual silhouette score lies within [-1,+1]. Positive values indicate that a point is closer on average to its own cluster than to the nearest alternative. Values near zero indicate weak separation between these alternatives; negative values suggest that the point is closer to another cluster. They do not establish whether an assignment is clinically correct. Individual silhouette values are defined in Equation 2.17, where a(i) is the mean intra-cluster dissimilarity for observation i and b(i) is its mean dissimilarity to members of the nearest alternative cluster. The average silhouette is the mean of all s(i) values and serves as the principal internal evaluation measure in this thesis. Noise percentage is also reported: it describes the proportion of observations left unassigned by density clustering, and thus its coverage.

Because they can identify elements of structure in large, high-dimensional data sets, UMAP and HDBSCAN have found application in fields such as computational biology and associated disciplines.

For assessing whether or not the structuring of clusters identified by these methods is appropriate when there is no known "gold standard" against which to measure them, the present study employs an approach that incorporates a combination of internal validation techniques, external consistency measures and sensitivity analyses. These approaches allow indirect assessment of the validity of these results.

Comparing cluster solutions produced from similar data, such as cluster assignments that were developed using different imputation methods, can be accomplished through determining an appropriate level of agreement between partitions. A commonly used method to accomplish this is through the utilization of the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) [Hubert and Arabie, 1985] in comparing the pair-wise cluster assignments to determine the amount of agreement above what would occur by chance.

To utilize the formula shown in Equation 2.18, we must first identify two clusterings of n objects denoted as U = {U_i} and V = {V_j}. We will also need to identify contingency counts denoted as n_ij = |U_i ∩ V_j|, where i and j index the clusters in U and V. The marginal totals denoted as a_i = ∑_j n_ij represent the number of elements in U_i. The marginal totals denoted as b_j = ∑_i n_ij represent the number of elements in V_j.

The ARI has been defined so that when there is a perfect agreement between the cluster assignment it results in a value of +1. When the ARI is equal to zero it indicates that the agreement between cluster assignments corresponds to the chance baseline. When the ARI takes on a negative value it indicates that there was less agreement between cluster assignments than would have occurred at random [Robert et al., 2020].

I also use the Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) to quantify how much information one clustering provides about another, while normalizing this measurement based upon the entropy of the cluster label.

Utilizing the mutual information I(U;V) and Shannon entropies H(·) [Shannon, 1948] shown in Equation 2.19 will provide a result of 1 if all cluster assignments agree completely and a result of 0 if the cluster assignments are determined to be statistically independent.

To further understand how similar or different individual clusters are across two solutions, I use the Jaccard index. In Equation 2.20, A and B denote the sets of observations belonging to the clusters being compared. The index is the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union, so its values lie within [0, 1]. Larger values indicate greater similarity in membership.

I also use clusterwise stability matching [Hennig, 2007] to assess stability under resampling. In each of R resampling iterations, an original cluster C_k is paired with the resampled cluster whose Jaccard overlap with it is largest. The stability score for C_k is the mean of these maximum overlaps across iterations, as defined in Equation 2.21. A per-cluster score > 0.7 is used here as the stability criterion.

Together, NMI and ARI quantify agreement between two cluster solutions. They are agreement measures, rather than tests of statistical significance.

These data came from an actual clinical setting; therefore, when selecting tests, the neuropsychologist administering them used their professional judgment based on what they considered relevant for the clinical question being asked of them, as well as the ability of the patient to participate. This creates a patterned type of missingness for this data set. Many measures can be found on nearly every assessment; but, many others will only appear when specific clinical issues arise. Missingness therefore reflects clinical assessment choices, with rates across the available measures ranging from about 5% for screening tools to over 90% for specialized assessments.

In addition to variability in terms of percentage of missing values per measure, measures also vary in terms of scale (standardized z-scores/scaled scores/raw timed measures). The scales were aligned during domain aggregation (Section 3.4). In Table 4.1 I present the missingness distribution for the 14 candidate variables. Only 53.1% (9,245 assessments) of the 17,406 records had complete data for all 14 variables. Complete-case analysis would therefore exclude 46.9% (8,161 assessments) of the sample. The imputation approach (Section 3.3) is intended to retain these assessments and their observed clinical information.

All data have been deidentified using standard procedures to protect patients' confidentiality.

The data were drawn from a clinical neuropsychology database maintained by a rehabilitation center. There were 22,075 raw entries for 8,739 unique individuals, some of whom had been assessed on multiple occasions. Each assessment entry recorded 31 variables, including demographic and administrative data, injury details and neuropsychological test results in six cognitive areas: orientation, attention, visuospatial perception, language, memory and executive function. After Tier-1 filtering, as described in Section 3.2, there were 17,406 assessments remaining for 7,285 individuals in the final analyzed dataset.

The unit of observation for the historical portion of this analysis was the single assessment. The patient-level extension in Section 3.8 uses one index assessment per patient, selected as the earliest eligible assessment, and keeps the same patient split for trajectory modeling. In the historical clustering, imputation-comparison and assessment-level bootstrap analyses, follow-up assessments remained separate observations. They were not aggregated into larger units of analysis based on the 7,285 patients. Although this approach preserves the observed changes in a person's status over time, it does not take into account the dependence between successive assessments from the same individual. The stability estimates may therefore appear more precise than estimates from resampling grouped by patient. The principal exception among the historical analyses was the multinomial sensitivity analysis in Section 4.7, where both the training/test sets and bootstrap samples were grouped by patient.

In order to be selected as part of this study, an assessment needed to include at least one observed score among those 14 retained tests. Therefore, the 50% missingness threshold applied to the selection of variables, while a separate requirement for each assessment, the minimum number of observations, determined whether it was eligible for inclusion in the study.

This produced a data matrix including 17,406 assessments across 7,285 patients. Of these assessments, 16,553 had at least seven observed test scores, and 853 had fewer than seven. The sensitivity to the historical variable-selection threshold is discussed further in Section 4.10. The patient-level sensitivity analysis requiring a minimum of seven observed test scores is reported separately in Section 4.12. blocks.description: Calculating Scores for Each Cognitive Domain
blocks.tested_text: Domain scores were calculated as administration-frequency-weighted means of the variables representing each domain. Each variable j was given a weight w_j = 1 - r_j, where r_j represents the missingness rate, and the weights were normalized within domains. This gives greater weight to variables measured more frequently during routine care. It reduces the influence of sparsely measured variables, whose contributions would otherwise rely more heavily on imputed values. These weights cannot be interpreted as a measure of psychometric reliability: they do not estimate internal consistency, test-retest reliability or measurement error. Reducing the dimensionality from 14 individual variables to six domain scores gives distance-based methods fewer dimensions to operate over. A domain-level profile also allows clinicians to consider cognitive deficits in terms of cognitive domains rather than individual test variables. There is a trade-off. Two patients could receive an equivalent average memory score yet differ in what they can recall immediately versus after a delay. Hypothesis H4 assesses whether the reduction in redundancy and improvement in interpretability provide enough reason to accept that loss of detail.

blocks.tested_text: Each imputed dataset was processed through the same steps. First, it was scaled with a robust scaler. Second, I ran each UMAP hyperparameter combination across ten different random seeds, giving ten embeddings per combination. I picked the embedding with the highest silhouette score. These repeated runs assessed sensitivity to stochastic initialization; they were not folds of cross-validation. Third, I tested a grid of 120 HDBSCAN parameter configurations and selected the one with the highest quality score Q. This was a hyperparameter sweep, not 120-fold cross-validation. Fourth, observations that HDBSCAN had originally labeled as noise were assigned to the nearest substantive cluster using k-nearest-neighbour similarity (k = 10) in UMAP space. This relabeling yielded 100% coverage. It was allowed only when the silhouette decreased by less than 10%, to preserve separation between clusters.

In order to decide which configuration to retain, I assigned a composite quality score to all of these candidates. blocks.tested_text: Consider an illustrative assessment with twelve observed retained tests and missing scores for the timed attention task and delayed verbal recall. In the historical analysis, MICE fills the missing values. Direction alignment, standardization and domain weighting then produce six composite scores. These scores undergo robust scaling and transformation using UMAP before HDBSCAN assigns a density-based group. Eligible noise points receive the separate KNN reassignment described above. The resulting labels, Above-Average, Near-Normal and Global Impairment, describe severity relative to this cohort. The H2 agreement diagnostic is a separate fixed-reference analysis; it does not supply a clinical confidence score for this example. blocks.tested_text: H1 (Stability and Discreteness of Cognitive Clusters). I anticipate that, for the majority of imputation approaches, the UMAP + HDBSCAN pipeline will find at least two stable cognitive clusters. The stability criterion requires the best solution from at least eight of the ten methods to have a mean silhouette value greater than or equal to 0.40 and a noise proportion before reassignment less than or equal to 0.30. These thresholds assess partition quality and stability in the selected embedding. They do not, on their own, establish discrete cognitive phenotypes. Discreteness is also evaluated using the shape of the cluster profiles, principal-component structure, separation in the original six-domain space and sensitivity of the identified number of clusters.

H2 (Robustness Across Imputation Techniques). I expect reasonable to high agreement across imputation techniques with respect to group assignments when both the geometric representation and partition model are held constant. The UMAP + HDBSCAN pipeline remains my primary discovery method. For H2, the secondary agreement diagnostic uses a k-means labeling rule trained on the MICE embedding and applied without modification to the other imputations. The criterion for support is a median ARI greater than 0.50 across the 45 pairs of methods, with NMI reported as a complementary measure. There is flexibility in choosing a threshold; this one exceeds chance and indicates substantial overlap in cluster membership under a common projection and labeling rule. The hypothesis therefore evaluates the robustness of assignments under a fixed reference structure. It does not require or claim that separate fits of UMAP + HDBSCAN recover the same number of tiers.

H3 (Relationship Between Clinical Unit and Cluster Membership). I expect a relationship between cluster membership and clinical unit. To test this, I create contingency tables and compute chi-square statistics for independence for each imputation technique. Results supporting H3 would show a statistically significant association at α = 0.05 after Bonferroni correction, with Cramér's V greater than 0.10. As an additional sensitivity analysis for potential confounding, I conduct a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test while conditioning on an appropriate covariate.

Pairwise Agreement. To remove variability introduced by refitting other parts of the pipeline, I use a shared reference-pipeline strategy. This is a secondary sensitivity analysis; the primary tiers were discovered with UMAP + HDBSCAN. I train one StandardScaler, one UMAP model and one k-means model with k=3 on MICE-imputed domain scores. The remaining methods are standardized, projected through this MICE-trained pipeline and labeled using the same k-means model. The intention behind using k-means here is to provide a fixed labeling function, so that only the imputed values vary among methods. This design assesses whether assessments produced by different imputations fall into similar regions under a common embedding and partition. It does not test whether a newly fitted UMAP + HDBSCAN pipeline would recover the same geometry, density hierarchy or number of tiers from each imputed dataset. The resulting ARI (Equation 2.18) and NMI (Equation 2.19) matrices compare every method with every other method and are presented as heatmaps in Chapter 4. Agreement for each assessment is defined as follows:

High-consensus assessments are those assigned to the modal cluster by at least 0.8M = 0.8 × 10 = 8 methods. This agreement fraction is not a calibrated clinical probability.

Chi-Square Test, Cramér's V and CMH Test. A contingency table cross-classifies two categorical variables, such as cluster assignment and clinical unit, to give their joint counts. Pearson's chi-square test compares the observed counts O_ij with the expected counts E_ij under the assumption that the two variables are independent:

Here, O_i· and O_· j denote the row and column sums. With r rows and c columns, the test statistic is compared with a chi-square distribution having (r - 1)(c - 1) degrees of freedom to obtain the p-value. Cramér's V expresses the strength of association on a scale from zero to one, normalizing the chi-square statistic for sample size:

Patient-Grouped Multinomial Sensitivity Analysis. Since associations do not establish predictive performance, I compared two regularized multinomial logistic models for detailed clinical-unit assignment. The baseline model used the broad diagnostic categories provided by the clinical-unit lookup, while the augmented model also included cognitive-severity tier. Units representing fewer than 50 unique patients were combined into an "other units" category, resulting in 17 outcome classes. Five-fold stratified group cross-validation kept every assessment from the same patient within a single fold. Held-out multinomial log loss was the primary performance measure; accuracy and macro-F1 were reported descriptively. The difference in out-of-fold log loss was bootstrapped 1,000 times by patient. Since the broad diagnostic category and detailed clinical unit come from the same lookup, this model is a sensitivity analysis of incremental classification performance rather than independent external validation.

Variance Inflation Factor. VIF is used to evaluate the degree of multicollinearity in regression models. For a variable j, it is calculated using the following formula:

Here, R_j^2 is the coefficient of determination obtained by regressing j on all the other predictors. VIF values above 10 give grounds for concern about multicollinearity and affect interpretation at both the variable level and in subsequent domain-level analyses.

blocks.tested_text:
Figure 3.1 displays the entire pathway from imputed data to final cluster assignment. Before applying UMAP and HDBSCAN, I use robust scaling with the median and interquartile range to reduce sensitivity to extreme values in the neuropsychological assessments [Bellio et al., 2020; Pinsky and Klawansky, 2023]. Floor effects occur when severely impaired participants accumulate at the minimum end of an assessment's scale [Pinsky and Klawansky, 2023]. Ceiling effects occur where participants without impairments accumulate at the maximum end [Pinsky and Klawansky, 2023]. While robust scaling helps to reduce the influence of extreme values, it does not eliminate either type of mass. Scaling with the median and interquartile range may also magnify the effect of the tails of a distribution when its central range is narrow. I discuss this sensitivity in Section 4.12 and quantify its size.

UMAP followed by HDBSCAN was performed on every one of the twenty imputed datasets, representing ten methods and two feature representations. An embedding can reflect the geometric structure of the data as well as variation from UMAP's random initialization. To assess this, I repeated each hyperparameter combination ten times and selected the best embedding based on the silhouette score of its initial HDBSCAN clustering.

blocks.tested_text:
The general process used to evaluate the statistical hypotheses follows conventional statistical practice. Each evaluation compares the data with a null hypothesis H_0, representing a no-effect baseline. The p-value is the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained, assuming H_0 is true. Lower p-values indicate stronger evidence against H_0. A predetermined significance level of α = 0.05 is used as the threshold for rejecting it. A procedure producing 95% confidence intervals would include the population parameter in 95% of repeated random samples from the same population, using the same methodology.

Bootstrapping samples the observed data with replacement to provide a simulated approximation of a statistic's sampling distribution. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that distribution give the lower and upper bounds of the bootstrap confidence interval. A z-score measures the number of standard deviations by which a value differs from the mean of a specified reference distribution. For the psychological instruments used here, standardization permits comparisons of scores from different tests.

Cohen's guidelines for standardized differences describe d = 0.20 as a small effect, d = 0.50 as a medium effect and d = 0.80 as a large effect. Cramér's V is used to describe the strength of association in chi-square analyses. The descriptive benchmarks used here are V = 0.10 for a small effect, V = 0.30 for a medium effect and V = 0.50 for a large effect.

The imputation methods came from scikit-learn for KNN and NMF, fancyimpute for SoftImpute and expectation maximization (EM), miceforest for MICE and predictive mean matching (PMM), and missforest for MissForest. The denoising autoencoder (DAE) and variational autoencoder (VAE) were implemented in PyTorch. UMAP and HDBSCAN used the umap-learn and hdbscan libraries, respectively. Statistical tests were performed with scipy.stats and statsmodels, while validation metrics were calculated with scikit-learn. The analysis code, together with the dashboard, is available at <https://github.com/zkunos/thesis_project>.

blocks.tested_text: H4 (Clustering at Domain Level versus Variable Level). I anticipate that grouping cognitive features by their respective domains will make the clustering representation easier to interpret than using all the individual variables. I also anticipate that clusters based on the domain-level representation will show similar, or possibly improved, separation compared with clusters based on individual variables. H4 is supported if, for at least two of three measurements, the domain-level results are equal to or better than the variable-level results. These measurements are silhouette score, mean VIF and condition number. Higher silhouette scores indicate better separation of clusters. Lower values for VIF and condition number indicate fewer problems due to multicollinearity and better numerical conditioning. Agreement between imputation methods has already been assessed in H2, so the comparison of feature representations belongs exclusively to H4.

blocks.tested_text:
First, I fitted K-means and Gaussian mixture models as baselines for k=2 through k=6. Neither produced a clear discrete optimum. The K-means elbow had no pronounced break, and the silhouette was highest at k=2, decreasing as each additional group was introduced. These results motivated an examination of density structure; I did not treat them as evidence that natural cognitive classes existed.

Next, I selected HDBSCAN because it can find irregularly shaped dense regions, represent low-density observations as noise and evaluate cluster persistence over a hierarchy without requiring a fixed value of k. This combination seemed appropriate for routine clinical data, where boundary cases may not fit cleanly into a group. UMAP was run with ten random seeds per parameter configuration, and HDBSCAN was evaluated over the full grid of 120 configurations described in Chapter 3. The comparison of t-SNE and UMAP in Figure 4.4 is descriptive. It shows how the selected assignments appear under two projections, but it is not an independent test of whether clusters exist or are discrete.

For the UMAP + HDBSCAN combination, the hyperparameters I settled on were n_components=8, n_neighbors=15 and min_dist=0.0 for UMAP, allowing tight packing in the embedding space [McInnes et al., 2018]. For HDBSCAN, I used min_cluster_size=1000 and min_samples=50, with cluster_selection_method=eom and epsilon=0.0. I selected a large minimum cluster size so that only substantive groupings would be retained.

blocks.tested_text:
The radar plots below show the mean cognitive-domain score for each tier, expressed as a z-score relative to the cohort mean. The three polygons are almost concentric: all domains move together. The tiers therefore differ mainly in their overall level of performance, rather than in the shape of their profiles.

I also generated a random forest surrogate model that attempted to reproduce the tier assignments from domain scores. Gini importance was calculated for each domain to describe its contribution to reproducing those labels. The domains are correlated, and the labels were derived from the same scores. Consequently, attention's low Gini importance relative to orientation, visuoperception and language does not indicate that attention is clinically unimportant. The ranking is conditional on this particular fitted partition.

blocks.tested_text: The initial portion of this chapter describes the assessment-level outcomes, and Section 4.12 includes the patient-level extension. The previous supplementary comparisons using multiple imputation and complete cases combined raw test scores. In the extension, domains are instead constructed after direction alignment and standardization. As such, although they draw on the same underlying data, the two sets of results represent different preprocessing specifications. They should therefore not be compared directly with each other.

blocks.tested_text:
Hypothesis 3 evaluates whether cognitive-severity tier is associated with clinical-unit assignment. The chi-square test showed a statistically significant association (χ^2 = 911.3, p ≈ 4 × 10^-156), with Cramér's V=0.162. This is a small effect according to Cohen's descriptive guidelines, although it exceeds the specified cutoff of 0.10. Across five independent MICE imputations, mean Cramér's V was similar at 0.154. This is an across-imputation sensitivity summary, not a Rubin-pooled inferential estimate.

The stratified sensitivity analysis indicated that the association persisted after accounting for the broad diagnostic grouping supplied by the clinical-unit lookup. Those groupings come from the same lookup as the detailed unit assignments, so this finding should not be interpreted as independent predictive validation.

The patient-grouped multinomial analysis gave no clear evidence that tier improved classification of detailed clinical unit beyond the broad diagnostic grouping. Diagnosis-only log loss was 0.6064, compared with 0.6051 after adding tier. The improvement of 0.0013 had a 95% patient-bootstrap interval of [-0.0006,0.0031]. Accuracy was 0.7772 versus 0.7770, and macro-F1 was 0.476 versus 0.480. I therefore regard H3 as supported only as an association hypothesis. The present analyses do not establish added predictive value.

blocks.description: Hypothesis 2: Imputation Sensitivity Under a Fixed Partition
blocks.tested_text:
I also tested Hypothesis 2, which proposed considerable overlap among assignments from different imputation methods when the same incomplete dataset is evaluated under a fixed embedding and partition model. The primary tiers were found through UMAP + HDBSCAN. For the secondary sensitivity analysis, I fitted a StandardScaler, a UMAP model and a k-means labeling rule with k=3 once to the MICE-imputed domain scores. These fitted models were then applied to all the other imputed datasets. By holding the models constant, I could isolate variation in the imputed values. There were 45 pairs of methods. The mean ARI was 0.710 and the median was 0.739, with a range of 0.509–0.880. The mean consensus confidence was 0.929. For 86.2% of assessments, at least eight out of the ten methods agreed on an assignment.

Thus, H2 is supported as specified: assignments are robust across different methods of filling missing values under a given embedding and partition model. However, this does not establish that independently refitted UMAP + HDBSCAN pipelines recover identical density hierarchies. Full-pipeline solutions produced cluster counts ranging from k=3 to k=5. Similarly, five independently imputed full-pipeline runs produced counts ranging from k=3 to k=7. This variability is consistent with discretizing a continuum, although it does not in itself prove that interpretation.

blocks.tested_text:
As stated previously in Chapter 3, Tier-1 filtering and removing assessments without a cognitive measure yielded 17,406 assessment records for 7,285 patients. The resulting data matrix contained fourteen cognitive variables across six domains. A table listing the percentage of missing values for each variable is shown as Table 4.1.

Substantial variability exists in the availability of the data. Percentages of missingness range from 0.7% for orientation items to 27.8% for ATMTA. If only complete cases were used, 46.9% of the assessments would be lost to analysis, with a risk of selection bias [Rubin, 1976]. In order to avoid losing such a large portion of the eligible assessment sample, imputation was used.

A co-occurrence heatmap, not shown, indicated instances where sets of variables are missing at the same time. Although this shows structured missingness, it does not establish a missing-at-random mechanism [Rubin, 1976; Little and Rubin, 2019]. The dependency patterns support conditional imputation over naive substitution. Correlations among variables within a domain tend to be high compared with correlations across domains. Shared variance among cognitive measures is compatible with a general cognitive-ability component [Lezak et al., 2012], which the subsequent clustering analyses examine further.

Figure 4.1 provides a graphical illustration of the percentage of missing values by cognitive measure, arranged in decreasing order. Routine screening measures tend to have lower rates of missing values than specialized assessments, consistent with their typical use in clinical practice [Lezak et al., 2012].

Mean imputation behaves differently from the other methods because of the loss of variance associated with replacing missing values by a mean [Rubin, 1987]. The nine additional methods preserve the marginal distributions more closely. In the comparisons shown here, KNN and PMM retain more of the visible discrete structure than methods such as MICE, MissForest and EM, which give smoother continuous reconstructions.

Bootstrap Stability. The bootstrap stability of each imputation method is assessed at the assessment level with B = 50 resamples. Resampling is done by row, without grouping together the assessments made on the same patient. For every resample, I run HDBSCAN again on the cached UMAP embeddings and compute the pre-KNN noise proportion as well as the median silhouette (Equation 2.17). The pre-KNN noise proportion counts all observations that have been left without a cluster assignment at this stage:

This proportion is also an input to the quality function Q in Equation 3.4. In order for a method to meet the H1 criteria, it must have a median silhouette value greater than or equal to 0.40 and a pre-KNN noise proportion less than or equal to 0.30. At least eight out of ten methods must achieve both values. I additionally use Hennig's matching procedure on the pre-KNN labels to assess the stability of each cluster, with a Jaccard threshold of 0.7 [Hennig, 2007].

blocks.tested_text:
The hypothesis for this comparison was that domain-aggregate features could reduce redundancy and make interpretation easier, while maintaining separation comparable to the individual-variable approach. I compared cluster separation using silhouette scores and evaluated how well conditioned the feature spaces were using condition numbers. Finally, I used variance inflation factors (VIFs) to compare multicollinearity in the two representations.

When test scores were aggregated, the average silhouette increased to 0.481 from 0.473 (Figure 4.11). The greater change was in the conditioning of the feature space. Average VIF decreased from 2.77 to 1.88, and the condition number decreased from 61.7 to 11.8. High VIFs indicate multicollinearity. Correlated variables can influence the distance calculations used by UMAP and HDBSCAN, so lower VIFs indicate less redundancy after aggregation. In addition, grouping tests by cognitive domain makes the representation easier to relate to the constructs measured by those tests [Lezak et al., 2012].

Hypothesis 4 is supported mainly by reduced redundancy and better numerical conditioning and interpretability. The small difference in silhouette scores does not indicate a meaningful improvement in cluster separation.

blocks.tested_text:
A random forest surrogate was created from the MICE-imputed domain scores, with the existing tier labels used as targets. It had an accuracy of 99.4% in five-fold cross-validation. This indicates that the partition boundaries defined from those same scores can be reproduced. It does not independently demonstrate natural cluster separation or predict clinical outcomes.

Gini importance ranked orientation highest (0.486), followed by visuoperception (0.237), language (0.171), memory (0.061), attention (0.028) and executive function (0.018), as shown in Figure 4.12. Permutation importance also placed orientation, visuoperception and language first, although attention was ranked lowest. These results describe the variables that reproduce the selected labels. When predictors are correlated, their contributions may overlap or substitute for one another, affecting both rankings [Boulesteix et al., 2012]. Thus, low surrogate importance does not necessarily mean that a predictor is irrelevant in a clinical context. The domain profiles and principal-component results in Section 4.4 provide additional information about the severity gradient.

blocks.tested_text:
H2 and Multiple Comparison Correction. In order to test H2, I performed forty-five pairwise comparisons of ARI values against a cutoff greater than 0.50. I applied Holm-Bonferroni adjustment to control family-wise Type I error and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment to control the false discovery rate. The null hypothesis was rejected for forty-four of the forty-five pairs using a parametric one-sided bootstrap p-value for each pair under both correction methods. The remaining pair was KNN–SoftImpute, with a mean bootstrap ARI of 0.509 and a 95% confidence interval of [0.497, 0.521]. All pairs except this borderline case therefore showed agreement significantly above the specified cutoff.

Across-Imputation Sensitivity Summary. I generated M = 5 independent MICE imputations and ran the full pipeline on each. For each nonlinear statistic, I present the across-imputation mean Q̅ and a descriptive dispersion interval, defined by Q̅± t_0.975,4√((1+1/M)B), where B is the sample variance of the five estimates. This interval describes only between-imputation variation. No within-imputation variance was estimated. Given this limitation and the nonlinear nature of Cramér's V and silhouette, the intervals are not interpreted as Rubin-rule confidence intervals. They instead provide sensitivity summaries describing how the results vary across plausible imputations. Mean Cramér's V across imputations was 0.154, with a descriptive interval of [0.049, 0.259]. The mean silhouette gap was 0.050 [0.043, 0.058]. The number of recovered clusters ranged from three to seven, and domain-level features outperformed variable-level features in each of the five runs.

blocks.tested_text: Hypothesis 1 contains two related claims. First, that reproducible groups can be found in the assessment data. Second, that these groups represent discrete cognitive phenotypes. In order to examine stability, I used fifty bootstrap resamples for each of the imputation methods. For every resample, I fitted HDBSCAN again on the resampled UMAP embedding and collected three measures: silhouette, pre-KNN noise proportion and Hennig core-Jaccard matching. The noise proportion was recorded before the KNN reassignment step. This gave a bootstrap distribution of the measures for each method, shown in Figure 4.6. These distributions allow the methods to be compared, with their exact summaries reported in Table 4.2.

Listwise Deletion Baseline. When I had removed the 46.9% of assessments that included missing values, I then ran the pipeline using the remaining 9,245 complete cases. This produced two clusters with a silhouette measure of 0.257. Moderate agreement existed between the MICE solution for these same assessments and the solution derived by only using complete case data (ARI = 0.625; NMI = 0.519). However, they were clearly not equivalent. Therefore, imputation has an impact on the analysis: removing 46.9% of assessments alters both the number and quality of tiers found in the analysis.

Subsampling Stability. For the twenty randomly chosen 80% assessment subsamples, the mean pairwise ARI was 0.273 and the median pairwise ARI was 0.277. Fifteen of the fits resulted in a two-cluster recovery, and three resulted in a three-cluster recovery. Two fits resulted in no clustering. Therefore, there exists a substantial level of sensitivity regarding the historical UMAP + HDBSCAN tiering assignment as it pertains to resampling. The results reported above relate to individual assessment rows, and should not be confused with the separate patient-level k-means stability experiment described in Section 4.12.

blocks.description: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text: The historical analysis found broad cognitive-severity structure within the overall group of individuals who had sustained an acquired brain injury (ABI). However, the patient-level extension found reproducible score groupings whose membership depended on scaling and imputation. Together, these analyses neither establish sharply discrete clinical phenotypes nor prove that such phenotypes are absent. In determining which historical assessments fell into the "above-average", "near-normal" and "global-impairment" tiers, I considered how they performed across the entire battery. It is important to note that while the tiers have different levels, they do not have different shapes. Each of the six domains moved in the same direction. This is demonstrated through Figure 4.5. One principal component explained approximately 56 percent of the total variability seen in the domain scores. Further, it loaded positively for all six domains at nearly identical magnitudes. Therefore, I believe the results indicate a stratification by level of severity, rather than identifying separate cognitive profiles. The tiers were also related to clinical unit placement (see §4.7) however, no additional predictive value was shown from this analysis over and above the broad diagnostic grouping.

Initialization and Resampling. The historical parameter search repeats UMAP initialization. Silhouette-based seed selection is an aspect of model selection rather than independent validation. Gaussian Mixture / Latent Profile Baseline. To allow for a model-based approach to comparing the classification methods, I fitted Gaussian mixture models (with full covariance matrices) to the imputed domain scores for k = 2 through 6. This represents a form of latent profile analysis, but it is not a formal latent profile analysis that uses full-information maximum likelihood estimation on the incomplete raw data. As k increased, the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) decreased from 243,249 when k=2 to 92,606 when k=6. There were no BIC optima found within the k values that I tested. Therefore, I view the mixture-models as providing an inconclusive answer regarding the number of classes. The continuum representation depends heavily on the concentric nature of the domain profiles, the dominance of the first principal component, the lack of strong original space silhouettes and the dependence of the number of tiers upon the specific method used. The observed-data mixture extension in Section 4.12 subsequently fits the incomplete test matrix directly, with a wider range of restricted distributional families.

blocks.description: Imputation Sensitivity Under a Fixed Partition
blocks.tested_text: I regard Hypothesis 2 as the main methodological contribution, while defining its scope narrowly. I used UMAP + HDBSCAN for the initial discovery of the primary clusters. Following this, I applied a separate fixed-reference diagnostic, using a single k-means fit on the MICE embedding and projected all the other imputed datasets into that same structure. As such, point assignments changed very little when comparing imputation methods under this diagnostic: the 45 method pairs yielded an average ARI greater than 0.70, and all 45 pairs had an ARI greater than 0.50 (§4.6). I therefore consider the relatively easy recovery of structure as evidence for a strong severity gradient whereas the more difficult to recover multi-dimensional profile structure represents less of an easily identifiable and possibly fragile structure. This distinction likely explains the robustness while still allowing for method-specific variability [Rubin, 1987].

blocks.description: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text: In addition to providing insights into an important concern with the field of neuropsychology — the degree to which differences across a variety of test batteries reflect variation associated with the domain tested vs. a general factor — the current findings also demonstrate how large a proportion of the recoverable structure in this routinely collected cohort is explained by the general severity dimension. Secondary domain-specific variation was present, but I did not find that it determined the clustering. Therefore, it appears from these results that there is support for both clinical experience (whereby global impairments are used initially to separate patients before grouping them by more narrow dissociation patterns) [Maas et al., 2017], and the positive manifold of inter-test correlation typically seen in neuropsychological research [Lezak et al., 2012]. These findings suggest that the results obtained in terms of phenotyping here provide a somewhat conservative account of the phenomenon being examined compared to other investigations. For example, under imputation-robust, sensitivity-tested conditions, overall severity emerged before specific profile patterns. I do not place too much emphasis on this lack of finding: given that domain aggregation and density clustering occur on manifolds where a general factor is dominant, there is limited sensitivity to detect narrow dissociations, including an attention-specific subgroup, if these are small or orthogonal to the principal severity gradient.

blocks.description: Imputation Sensitivity Under a Fixed Partition
blocks.tested_text:
Although I believe the way in which I addressed the imputed data impacted the number of tiers that were discovered as well as the quality of these tiers, I also have reason to think that my findings concerning where patients lie along the cognitive-severity signal may be less dependent upon the type of imputation strategy used. In general terms, the fixed-reference diagnostic preserves many assignments across the compared imputations. This claim does not carry over unchanged to independent model fitting: the new KNN sensitivity gives an ARI of 0.538 against the reference three-group partition. While I do not view these results as suggesting that one could simply ignore the presence of missing data, I would suggest that researchers approach missingness systematically and provide information about the methodology they employed, and clinicians consider tier labels as tools to assist them in making clinical judgments and decisions, but not as substitutes for clinical education/training/experience.

The distinction between smooth, model-based (i.e., EM, DAE, VAE), versus local donor-type (e.g., KNN), imputation methods was quite clear (see Figure 4.9). Although some literature has classified various imputation methodologies into categories such as machine learning/statistical/deep learning, it appears to me that a better way to classify these methodologies is by distinguishing between the "smooth" family of models, where imputed values tend to be smoothed toward a model-based conditional mean; and local/donor models where a small number of neighbors (donors) are utilized to estimate missing values for a given assessment.

To determine how resilient the findings regarding the hypotheses were, I conducted additional testing. 
First, I used a listwise deletion baseline; Second, I did a subsample stability test. Third, I made bootstrap confidence intervals. Fifth, I included both the number of days post-injury and within-patient tier transitions (i.e., moves upward or downward) per subject. Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. With respect to an assessment level sampling approach, the mean ARI for H2 = 0.710; 95% CI [0.702, 0.717]; for H3, Cramér’s V = 0.166; 95% CI [0.156, 0.175]; and for H4, silhouette gap = -0.002; 95% CI [-0.021, 0.013]. In addition, as this resampling is assuming each of the 17,406 assessments to be independent of one another and ignoring the interdependence of each of the assessments in terms of their association with a common group of seven thousand two hundred eighty-five patients, the confidence intervals provided via this type of resampling may be too narrow and should not be interpreted as patient-grouped uncertainty.

With application of Holm-Bonferroni correction across the 45 pairs of comparisons (as described in Section 4.10) 44 of the 45 pairs rejected the null hypothesis that ARI ≤ 0.50. blocks.description: Cognitive Structure and the Limits of Phenotype Claims
blocks.tested_text:
My findings are not contrary to research concerning the presence of multiple dissociable cognitive profile types post-brain injury (e.g., [García-Rudolph et al., 2021]), yet my study qualifies how one interprets data from such research. My pipeline differed from those studies in several ways. First, UMAP + HDBSCAN is capable of processing non-convex structure and low-density "noise". Second, the bootstrap analysis allowed me to assess the reproducibility of clusters under assessment resampling. Third, I standardized, winsorized and direction-aligned each variable before forming composites. Each of these preprocessing choices matters. For example, if you have high variance raw scores (i.e., a subject's completion times for the Trail Making Test) which disproportionately influence your raw composite; non-cognitive variables creating false axes; nearly empty records distorting density estimates; what appears to be differences in phenotype may simply represent artifact of the pre-processing techniques and not true structural differences in neuropsychology. Chapter 6 explores this issue further.

Hypothesis One is only partially supported (see Section 4.5). All ten imputation methods demonstrated both adequate levels of silhouette and noise metrics. Therefore, all ten imputation methods successfully recovered ordered bands of severity. However, overall core Jaccard ranged from 0.509 to 0.630. Individual matched-cluster values ranged from 0.383 to 0.633. Also, the number of recovered clusters varied from three to five. While these results suggest ordered severity bands exist, they do not suggest that sharply discrete, uniformly reproducible phenotypes exist. Boundary movement can occur without disrupting the underlying severity order.

To see if the clinical-unit assignment was related to cognitive-severity tier, I ran a test to check for an association (contingency) in terms of "tier" (cognitive-severity level) and "unit". There was a statistical association found; however, according to Cohen, there was a small effect size. After conducting a stratified sensitivity analysis controlling for the broader diagnostic category provided by the unit look-up (both categories are derived from the same look-up), the association was still found to be statistically significant. Since both the broad group and the detailed group come from the same source, I would not consider that finding to represent independently validated results.

Although the association could have some clinical relevance, it does not provide evidence regarding predictive ability or causality. In the patient-grouped multinomial sensitivity analyses, when tier was added to the previously identified broad diagnostic grouping, the held-out log loss changed from 0.6064 to 0.6051. However, through use of patient bootstrap improvement intervals, the improvement interval included zero. Accuracy was unchanged to three decimal places. Therefore, I conclude that H3 represents only that tier distributions differ across units. To assess whether the addition of severity tier will improve prospective routing or predictive performance of future outcomes, additional variables representing separate predictors, patient grouped validation data, and clinical outcomes collected for that purpose will be required.

There exist numerous ways in which one can describe cognitive characteristics. 
Two general methods include variable-level characteristics and aggregated characteristics. 
Variable-level features treat each individual test separately, while aggregate features are averages or sums of tests intended to measure a shared cognitive domain. I evaluated if aggregated characteristics of cognitive domains would be better conditioned than variable level characteristics. Better conditioning is defined as having lower multicollinearity with lower values for variance inflation factors (VIF) and a low condition number.

My data analysis provided support for H4. Although there was virtually no increase in cluster separation, my findings showed that domain-aggregated characteristics had lower multicollinearity than variable level characteristics. Specifically, while the silhouette value only changed slightly (0.473 to 0.481), the average VIF decreased from 2.77 to 1.88 and the condition number decreased from 61.7 to 11.8 (see Section 4.8). Therefore, I consider H4 as providing evidence that domain-aggregation will reduce redundancy and produce a more easily interpreted, better-conditioned representation of assessment data. However, it does not provide evidence of materially stronger clustering. This benefit also supports the practical application of evaluating test battery scores on a domain basis rather than score-by-score [Lezak et al., 2012].

blocks.tested_text: I want to highlight just one very important condition for aggregating test variables: the variable-level preprocessing steps must precede aggregation. Data must first be transformed (winsorized), aligned with respect to direction, and scaled (standardized) before data from each variable can be combined into a composite; otherwise, differences in their original scales will generate artificial results. As an example, if several memory tests were aggregated prior to standardizing them, then the resulting composite would likely reflect the performance on whichever test had the greatest range rather than reflecting whatever memory construct was being measured. Similarly, if multiple tests that have a high correlation entered into an unstandardized composite, UMAP and HDBSCAN could use the same cognitive dimension to exaggerate computation of distances. Aggregation produces one feature per domain; however, it does not ensure equal influence for the domains after further scaling. In addition, the patient-level extension demonstrates how robust scaling places greater emphasis upon language and orientation tails.

blocks.description: Feature Importance and What Drives Severity
blocks.tested_text:
In my opinion, the data in §4.9 provide a description of the relationships among the cognitive domains and the classification results from the Random Forest surrogate model. Since the Random Forest surrogate had an accuracy of 99.4% when the same domain scores used to assign labels were used, I believe that the ranking found by the Random Forest surrogate primarily reflects the recovery of the boundaries of the fitted partition, rather than explanatory structures underlying it. The random forest ranked orientation, visuoperceptual ability and language higher than attention and executive function, but I do not give this ordering a strong interpretation. As mentioned earlier, these domains are highly correlated, and Gini importance is susceptible to variability under correlated predictors [Boulesteix et al., 2012].

In contrast, I have much more confidence in the reliability of the principal component analysis. One component accounted for 56% of the total variance in the domain scores, and the six domains had similar magnitudes in terms of their positive loadings on this factor. I interpret this finding as consistent with a general severity dimension rather than domain-specific dissociation or some attention-specific pattern of performance within this particular domain-aggregated pipeline. The robustness checks contained in §4.10 demonstrate large variations in assignments due to subsampling of assessments and changes in tier count with variable-inclusion thresholds. These results highlight the need for researchers who conduct data-driven research on phenotyping to clearly document how they preprocessed their data and also to perform sensitivity analyses in addition to reporting their primary results.

blocks.tested_text:
I understand the current study findings as supportive of a three-tiered cognitive severity stratification model. Nonetheless, I can see a number of constraints in using such an approach. In my opinion, the primary clinical implications are conservative; these tiers will potentially help summarize relative cognitive severity; however, they cannot be considered as independent clinical decision-making strategies. Ultimately, when patients enter the rehabilitation services system, their placement will still depend upon the medical education, knowledge of local services and professional expertise of the clinician making the placement. At present, I do not think these results justify direct clinical implementation beyond careful interpretation of cognitive severity and transparent handling of missing data.

Clinical professionals have traditionally utilized a visual analysis of the distribution of patient scores to determine which patients represent "unusual" cases. Similarly, based on the findings reported here, I support the continued use of both algorithms for cluster identification and visual observation to identify unusual cases. For many assessments included in the study, there were no clearly defined boundaries between distinct groups. Therefore, I would categorize the central tier of cognitive severity as being consistent with a boundary region cut from a continuum. Most patients fall along a broad severity gradient rather than within sharply separated natural categories. Thus, I believe that future tools should focus on identifying those assessments that are difficult to cluster and/or near the boundary of two adjacent regions/clusters; rather than forcing every assessment into a definitive phenotype label.

The new experiments answer the practical question of whether repeatable clusters can be obtained. Two-group k-means was selected for each of the 20 imputation screens, and its average validation agreement was 0.959. Three-group k-means was also repeatable under the same representation (ARI 0.935), including patient subsampling. This extends the earlier fixed-reference H2 diagnostic by independently refitting partitions while keeping validation patients fixed. The different cohort and feature construction prevent interpreting the larger ARI as an improvement over the historical value of 0.710.

Thus, even though repeatability and phenotype validity are distinct issues, equal-domain scaling resulted in substantial changes to the three-group assignments (ARI 0.243 against robust scaling), and imputation stability was reduced. Missing memory and executive tests were concentrated in some groups. Therefore, although a partition may be very reproducible it may still reflect aspects of both the score geometry and the test-administration process. The strong language contrast between at least one group in the robust-space clustering is a useful finding for description purposes, however, a clinically valid interpretation will require testing with other measurement and missingness models.

Firstly, the study was conducted at a single centre. As such, all data used in the study came from a single rehabilitation unit. This has created the potential for selection bias, and therefore, generalization to other clinical groups has not been established. The tests used have been extensively studied and have international validity, while the six cognitive domains provide a common framework for describing post-injury cognition. Multi-centre validation is still needed before treating this severity structure as a general characteristic of acquired brain injury (ABI), rather than a characteristic of this unit.

Secondly, most historical analyses treat the 17,406 assessments as separate observations rather than grouping them within the 7,285 patients. While repeated follow up assessments of the same patients are related (correlated) by definition, neither the primary clustering nor the assessment level bootstrap accounts for that relationship. Utilizing each individual assessment preserves the information contained in the clinical records regarding recovery status at each point in time, however, using each individual assessment could result in inflated estimates of cluster stability, and narrower confidence intervals than would exist if only patient grouped assessments were utilized. The patient-grouped multinomial sensitivity analysis addresses H3. The new extension provides additional discovery/validation techniques at the patient level, includes patient subsampling and integrated random-effects trajectories. It does not retroactively correct the uncertainty intervals from the historical assessment-level analysis.
