blocks.tested_text:
Thirdly, the recovered structure limits how we interpret our results. The historical data support the idea of a large range of severity gradations. However, the extension indicates that although reproducible partitions can exist among different representations of data, they remain sensitive to the specific representation used. Also, the analyses presented here do not allow us to determine a unique categorical structure. Most of the cohort lies along a single dimension representing overall cognitive severity. This is evident in that PC1 accounts for 56% of the total variation present. The three tiers represent a discretization of this continuum. Therefore, the tiers should not be considered as phenotypically separate entities with clearly delineated boundaries. The number of tiers will depend upon both how we define the thresholds for clusters and what proportion of the data is missing. It is also important to note that assessments that occur very close to the boundary lines of these tiers should be treated with caution. Ultimately, a continuous severity score may be more representative than discrete tiers (Section 6.2).

Fourthly, the analytical methods have a limited ability to examine changes over time. As indicated earlier, ABI recovery typically occurs rapidly during the early stages and then follows a slower rate thereafter [Ponsford et al., 2014; Maas et al., 2017]. Therefore, an individual assessment represents only a snapshot of a particular patient's recovery process at a particular point in time. Many individuals in the dataset include multiple assessments which allows researchers to evaluate whether there was evidence of change within individuals; however, the timing of when follow-up assessments were administered varies widely depending on clinical necessity rather than through the use of standardized procedures.

These likelihood results provide a complementary view. The restricted t mixtures fit the incomplete observations better than the selected Gaussian alternatives, but both families favored eight components at the search boundary. So, they are useful for describing distributions, but they do not identify an optimal number of patient types. As well, the improvement in trajectory likelihood with additional classes was unable to find a class combination that satisfied the rules regarding the minimum size of each class. Neither result demonstrates the absence of small subgroups.

The above results fit questions raised by recent incomplete data, ensemble and longitudinal research [Tong and Tortora, 2025; Tomo et al., 2026; Julià et al., 2026] which used some of the same concepts used here. However, this study uses a different implementation and a different cohort than the previous studies. This study shows that reproducible cognitive-score groupings exist under specified analytical choices. However, it does not confirm distinct clinical phenotypes. A comparison using independent outcomes of continuous scores alone versus scores plus group membership, followed by external replication, is needed before we will know if assigning patients to pre-determined categories provides useful additional information.

blocks.tested_text:
Within the sample of 5,206 patients that have longitudinal data (Section 4.10) - 50.2% remain in the same tier through all their study visits. Of the smaller sub-set of 912 patients with exactly two assessments and a tier change, there was a larger number of patients whose tiers moved up in scoring (n=706) than those whose tiers moved down (n=206). These results are compatible with recovery; however, tier movement is not a functional outcome. Other factors contributing to tier movement include selection, discharge, timing of study visits and changes in test availability.

Further longitudinal studies will need to be conducted using standardized time frames for assessments to answer this question.

A second factor limiting our ability to interpret these findings is the way we imputed missing values. It has been shown that the MAR assumption can't be evaluated based solely on observed data [Rubin, 1976; Little and Rubin, 2019]; missing test scores may occur when a patient is unable to complete them, thus providing information about the missing score. In cases where there is a MNAR mechanism for missingness, imputation could produce an overly optimistic estimate of test performance. Our comparisons did not provide a ceiling estimate of this type of bias. To evaluate possible deviations from our working missingness assumptions, we plan to conduct a formally defined delta shift sensitivity analysis.

Structured co-occurrence of missingness is compatible with test-battery protocols, but does not distinguish protocol-driven from outcome-dependent non-completion. Across ten imputation methods, at least 80% of methods agreed on the assignment for 86.2% of assessments under a fixed MICE-fitted rule. While this supports conditional assignment robustness, it does not support either the idea that missingness is ignorable or that multiple independent pipelines can identify the same groupings of individuals.

blocks.tested_text:
A key aspect of assessment eligibility was that at least one retained test had to have been observed, enabling a record with many missing entries to be included in the analysis. The stricter seven-observed-test sensitivity retained 6,602 index patients, with an adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.903 against the reference three-group assignments on shared validation patients. This shows some robustness to sparse-record exclusion; however, the unobserved cognitive status of excluded encounters remains uncertain.

The new observed-data mixtures directly address a deficiency within the historical impute-then-cluster approach by integrating missing coordinates. These mixtures still assume ignorable missingness, their continuous distributions approximate discrete and bounded scores, and their dispersion floor regularizes singular solutions. Four of the 32 fits failed to achieve the requested convergence tolerance, and both selected t families reached the maximum of eight components. A unique class count therefore remains unidentified. Skew-t and multivariate contaminated longitudinal models were not implemented.

Feature engineering is still relevant. Non-cognitive features are removed, and test direction and scale are aligned before winsorization and aggregation into composite scores. These choices can produce artificial profile differences. The general methodological lesson is clear: unsupervised phenotyping depends upon preprocessing. Any distinctive phenotype identified through exploratory methods should be evaluated relative to how variables were scaled, which variables were chosen for inclusion, and how the study population was defined before receiving a clinical label.

blocks.tested_text:
HDBSCAN adds the challenge of sensitivity to hyperparameters. The search evaluates 9×120 parameter configurations using the composite quality metric Q. Because Q includes silhouette and the UMAP seed is chosen partly on silhouette, the degree of separation shown in the selected embedding is optimistic by construction. It is a selected internal statistic, rather than an unbiased estimate of cluster quality. PCA suggests one major axis related to cognitive severity, with PC1 accounting for 56% of the variance. Yet the historical assessment-subsampling mean ARI of 0.273 shows that exact assignments can vary substantially when the sample changes. These findings do not provide a definitive answer about a uniquely correct categorical partition.

Computational cost presents a further practical limit. Running UMAP + HDBSCAN fifty times per method is computationally intensive. However, the modular design allows parallel processing, which kept runtime costs manageable on a typical consumer-grade laptop.

blocks.tested_text:
The extension also includes particular validation limits. Feature selection was inherited from the historical full cohort. Equal-domain scaling, established after assessing discovery variances, was an exploratory sensitivity. High ARI across bounded Bayesian imputations remains dependent upon that model and does not resolve MNAR. Cluster membership is related to test availability and neither of the domain-weighted methods have been clinically validated. The reference Gaussian-copula is estimated from these same data and samples missingness independent of values. Its tail fractions are descriptive rather than an omnibus calibrated significance test. The separated positive control was not a power study, and no calibrated Silverman test was implemented. Consensus summaries created from validation-assignment vectors are not separately validated prediction models.

Lastly, the previous supplementary comparison of complete-case and multiple imputed datasets used raw-test aggregation. In contrast, the patient-level extension aligns test direction and scale prior to aggregation. Controlled comparisons measure sensitivity to this difference but do not recalculate all previous statistics using the standardized-domain specification. As such, those previously calculated statistics are unable to validate the patient-level preprocessing pipeline.

blocks.tested_text:
Four potential areas for future work arise from the findings and limitations described above.

Firstly, one implication of the cognitive-severity gradients is that continuous cognitive-severity indices (derived through PCA, or learned using supervised learning on functional outcome metrics) could potentially produce more accurate representations of patient status and serve as more effective summary representations than categorical tiers. Therefore, future studies should compare continuous cognitive-severity indices with tiered classification systems in terms of predictive ability for prognosis and for determining appropriate intensity of rehabilitation based on need while considering tiered classification as a meaningful discrete representation of continuous data rather than inherent categories.

Secondly, extending the linear random-effects mixture model to assessments collected at regular time points would enable researchers to study how individuals’ recovery trajectories develop longitudinally; specifically, if patients’ position on the cognitive-severity gradient when first assessed relates to long-term outcomes, and whether different recovery rates exist among varying levels of severity [Ponsford et al., 2014]. The selection of this trajectory subset was determined by visit availability and follow-up duration. There remains much to examine such as non-linear changes, informative dropout, and external functional outcomes. The current analysis does not yet establish the prognostic or rehabilitation planning value of these trajectory subsets.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
Thirdly, multi-center validation is an important requirement for cognitive-severity stratification to be considered a feature of acquired brain injury (ABI) rather than this specific service. A multi-center approach comparing the results of multiple healthcare services and populations, and the various methods used for assessing cognition would assess whether the one-dimensional cognitive severity gradient described herein is consistent in populations with varying demographics, test-batteries, and assessment-schedules [Maas et al., 2017].

Fourthly, inclusion of neuroimaging data will facilitate the determination of how the degree of cognitive impairment post ABI relates to the underlying neurological mechanisms. By correlating an individual's location on the cognitive-severity gradient with structural and functional imaging metrics, researchers may identify neural substrates associated with global cognitive impairments after ABI. Such knowledge may also guide intervention development [Saatman et al., 2008; Maas et al., 2017].

blocks.tested_text:
This thesis tests whether neuropsychological scores for people with acquired brain injury contain reproducible cognitive structure despite incomplete testing. The historical assessment-level analysis and the patient-level extension support repeatable score groupings under specified analytical choices. Neither provides evidence for clinically distinct phenotypes nor proves that no subgroups exist.

Historically, the UMAP + HDBSCAN solution identified three severity groups from 17,406 assessments: Above Average (38.6%), Near Normal (36.4%), and Global Impairment (25.0%). For this study H1 is partially supported; although certain solutions meet both the silhouette and noise criteria using the embedded method, core Jaccard agreement was moderate, and number of clusters varied depending on which method was utilized. A dominant principal component and weak original-domain separation support a broad severity interpretation within that representation.

H2 is supported within its fixed-reference design. Applying a common MICE-fitted scaling, UMAP and three-group k-means structure to other imputations gave a mean pairwise ARI of 0.710. ARI represents assignment sensitivity as determined by a fixed rule. It does not imply identical independently discovered density hierarchies. Historical assessment-bootstrap uncertainty ignores patient dependence. The supplementary multiple-imputation and complete-case comparisons were performed using raw test aggregation, thus, they provide limited comparisons to the standardized-domain extension.

blocks.tested_text: H3 is supported in that clinical unit and tier are associated at the level of Cramér's V = .162. While adding tier to the broader diagnostic grouping improved patient-grouped validation log loss slightly over using only the broad groupings, the improvement interval included zero. H4 was generally supported via conditioning, since domain aggregation reduced the mean VIF from 2.77 to 1.88 and the condition number for the data from 61.7 to 11.8, although there was also a very slight increase in silhouette measure (from .473 to .481).

blocks.tested_text:
The extension included 7,285 index patients, split into 5,828 discovery and 1,457 validation patients. Two-group k-means was selected in all 20 stochastic-imputation screens, with mean pairwise validation ARI .959. When using fixed three-group k-means, the average ARI was .935 over imputations, and .968 across 50 patient subsamples. Therefore, the study determined reproducible grouping of the cognitive measures.

However, sensitivity to representation is the defining characteristic: when switching from robust to equal-domain scale, the three-group classification assignments (ARI = .243) changed substantially. Following application of robust scale, language and orientation accounted for most of the total variance of the dataset, while missingness in memory and executive test data was related to group classification. Therefore, high repeatability based upon a single preprocessing and imputation model does not imply stable clinical categories.

Using restricted robust t mixtures resulted in a better observed-data fit than did either of the alternative Gaussian models; although both of the selected t families also identified eight components at the search limit. However, because of the weak separation in the six-domain space, as well as ambiguity with respect to identifying the correct number of components, it would appear to preclude assigning eight distinct phenotype labels. From the 2,013 patients that qualified for longitudinal modeling techniques, the addition of extra trajectories improved likelihood. However, the inclusion of these groups resulted in groups below the specified 5% expected-membership threshold. Consequently, this rule reduced the model back down to a one-class random-effects model, thus still leaving unexplained nonlinear variability, and unresolved very small subgroupings.

blocks.tested_text:
The combination of workflows distinguishes robustness of fixed-reference assignment from independent refitting, patient resampling, geometric properties of features and the fit of models to observed data. Shared preprocessing aligns test direction and scale before tests are combined by domain. Original-space metrics, posterior uncertainty, model convergence, conditional consensus and trajectory eligibility are all reported explicitly. The computational implementation has been validated with a numerical approach. Clinical validation would require further work beyond this study.

In order to meet the inclusion criteria for the primary cohort, all assessments must include at least one observed retained test. An additional sensitivity analysis which required seven observed tests was performed to assess how the exclusion of sparse data (profiles) impacts cluster stability. This distinction makes the role of assessment completeness explicit when interpreting cluster stability.

blocks.description: Implications for Research and Clinical Interpretation
blocks.tested_text:
Continuous cognitive summaries and descriptive groups remain candidates for future outcome validation. Current labels should be accompanied by their preprocessing definition and uncertainty. They should not dictate treatment intensity or rehabilitation routing. While neither an association with clinical units nor multiple assessments of cognition alone can be used to indicate whether treatments produce outcomes that are clinically relevant, CogDash represents both of the analytical design alternatives for research, including their limitations for interpreting results and profile comparisons of saved models.

Empirical priorities for the next step in research will involve comparing independently-assessed outcome measures using continuous scores versus scores plus cluster membership; assessing the sensitivity of the observed effects to missing data, particularly when it is informative, and to procedures used in test administration; and replicating the observed relationships across other testing locations and scheduling times. Nonlinear longitudinal models and assessment of adequately measured small subgroups may provide a basis for future research without assuming that additional mixture components correspond to legitimate patient types.

Reproducible groupings of cognitive scores were identified in this sample. The memberships within those groups, and the number of such groups identified, depend on scaling, treatment of missing values, and choice of model family. This study provides evidence for a broad framework for describing cognitive ability, while providing many avenues for further investigation related to subgroups of cognition; however, clinical phenotypes that are distinct from one another, and which have been shown to add value in terms of clinical utility, remain unconfirmed.

blocks.tested_text: An exploratory extension of the current investigation was conducted on October 15, 2026. The primary objective of this examination was to evaluate if the historical severity groups contained reproducible subgroups as determined by various representations, missing-data assumptions and sampling units. This study is a supplement to H1-H4, but does not redefine them. The literature referenced to support this study was limited to journal articles published during the time period of October 15, 2025 through October 15, 2026. Methodological comparisons involving mixture models for missing data, multiple-imputation ensembles and methods to diagnose clusterability (as well as comparative longitudinal analysis) were informed by [Tong and Tortora, 2025; Tomo et al., 2026; Neville et al., 2026; Julià et al., 2026]. The findings indicating distortion within UMAP embeddings provided further justification for assessing the representation within measured feature space [Chen et al., 2026]. These articles motivate methodological comparisons; none validate a specific ABI subtype or establish that a proposed method will outperform the historical pipeline.

blocks.tested_text:
The eligible cohort included 17,406 assessments from 7,285 patients across the 14 retained cognitive tests. Patient identifiers linked repeated observations, with no duplicate patient-assessment-time pairs. There was no validated identifier available for identifying episodes of injury. However, one patient was found to have reported different ages of injury upon data collection and that patient was eliminated from the development of trajectories using their assessment history.

Each patient’s earliest eligible assessment is used in the cross-sectional portion of this research after ordering assessments by time since injury. Source row ordering is employed as a deterministic means to break ties when assessing which observation occurs first. Using a fixed random split (using seed number 20261015), 5,828 patients were assigned to the discovery group and 1,457 patients were placed into the validation group. Each patient contributes one index profile, so no patient appears in both sets. This estimates structure in patient index profiles, whereas the historical analysis describes assessment states across follow-up. As previously mentioned, the 14 variables selected for use in this research were inherited from the full cohort of patients who participated in the initial historical analysis. Therefore, the division described above does not provide an independent validation of how features were selected.

Additionally, eligibility required that at least one retained test be observed. A separate sensitivity analysis utilized index assessments where at least seven retained tests had been assessed to evaluate the effect of sparse measurement of patient assessment profiles.

blocks.tested_text:
Discovery data sets determine all of the statistical parameters for each test: the 1st percentile, 99th percentile, direction, mean and standard deviation. Values are then clipped to those percentile limits and the timed ATMTA scores are inverted. Tests are also standardized so that larger values represent better performance. The transformation leaves missing entries unchanged. For the completed-data branches, a bounded Bayesian chained-equations imputer was fit to discovery patients and used to impute missing values in validation patients. The deterministic reference model used 15 iterations. A sensitivity check with 50 iterations was performed to check convergence. It should be noted that this imputation process is different than the historical miceforest implementation and has its own set of modeling assumptions.

The completed standardized tests were aggregated into six domains based upon the frequency of administration of each test. Each domain’s weighting factor is based on the frequency of each test being administered to the discovery patients, but the factors were normalized at the level of each domain. The reference distance representation utilized domain medians and interquartile ranges (robust scaling), both derived from the discovery patients. The comparators used either the 14 completed tests or the five non-orientation domains. The five-dimensional PCA basis was calculated after removing one dimension which represented the first principal component derived from the discovery patient data. The residual representation is a diagnostic tool for exploring shape differences among profiles. As such it can potentially eliminate valid signal as well as common variance.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
An additional scaling sensitivity, introduced after inspecting discovery-set variances, scales every domain to a variance of 1. It assesses the influence of ceiling-heavy domains with narrow central ranges. By comparing identical label sets across both geometric models it is possible to isolate differences in the partition (the way data are grouped) versus differences in how silhouette is calculated. Each transformation on the validation patients remains constant at its estimate at the time of discovery.

At the level of the individual patient, the patient-level analysis uses clipping, direction alignment and test standardization prior to aggregating. Previous supplemental analyses utilizing multiple imputation and complete-case comparisons aggregated raw tests. As such, the previously reported results were based on a differing preprocessing specification. Therefore, controlled comparisons using the same completed test values quantify the effects of aggregation without recalculation of all previous H1-H4 statistics.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
K-means and sampled partitioning around medoids (PAM) were compared for values of k=2,…,8. The PAM algorithm employs CLARA-style sampling using three sets of 400 discovery patients, and then performs BUILD/SWAP optimization within each sample. Evaluations of Gaussian mixtures were performed for k=1,…,8 when employing either full or tied covariance matrices. HDBSCAN was applied directly to data using both of the following parameterizations: minimum cluster size of 100 or 300, and min_samples=20. A UMAP-based comparator employed three dimensions and 15 or 50 neighbors, as well as min_dist=0 before application of the identical HDBSCAN parameterization. Validation assignments used the fitted centers, medoids, mixture probabilities, or UMAP transformation and HDBSCAN's approximate prediction.

For each representation/method, the partition/density models were chosen based on the discovery silhouette and the Gaussian mixture models were chosen based on the discovery BIC, requiring convergence where applicable and at least two percent discovery membership in each group. Silhouette scores were calculated in the respective original representations, including for UMAP-derived labels. When computing discovery silhouettes, we utilized up to 2,000 sampled observations; when calculating validation silhouettes, we utilized all available validation assignments. Noise was excluded from silhouette, and coverage was reported separately. Scores from different feature geometries are not a common performance scale. Searching k≥2 by silhouette cannot establish that groups exist relative to a one-population model.

blocks.tested_text:
Incomplete-data mixtures were fitted directly to the 14 transformed tests by use of the EM algorithm. This algorithm was run with integration of missing coordinates as part of the observed data likelihood. The restricted families included: (a) Gaussian; (b) t distribution with 4 and 10 fixed degrees of freedom; and (c) contaminated normal with a 90% normal core and a tenfold covariance inflation for the remaining 10%. Each family was used with k=1,…,8, using two initializations, stopping after no more than 120 iterations or when the log-likelihood change fell below 10^-5 per observation, and imposing an eigenvalue floor on the dispersion matrix of 0.02. For the t family, this is a scale-matrix floor. Only mean filling was performed for the generation of these initial values. These Python implementations were numerically tested. They are restricted adaptations and do not reproduce the complete MixtureMissing package [Tong and Tortora, 2025].

Recorded were BIC, entropy-penalized ICL, convergence, validation observed-data log likelihood, and the posterior probabilities that each individual belonged to each component. Selected fits required convergence and at least 2% discovery membership in every component. Likelihood-based measures are only compared across fits which share the same transformation into a space of 14 dimensions. These continuous probability distributions approximate discrete and bounded score representations; therefore, additional components may represent ceiling effects, skewness or tails, instead of representing separate subpopulations among patients.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.description: Independent Refitting, Consensus and Cluster Tendency
blocks.tested_text: PCA/dip diagnostic results were then compared to a matched-size screening set consisting of 1,000 discovery patients and 100 single-Gaussian-copula reference datasets. Empirical discrete margins and resampled joint missingness masks were retained. Each reference data set was processed through the same steps as the initial processing of the discovery data set. These include preprocessing, imputing the missing data and running the k-means cluster analysis on each reference data set using k=2,…,8. Tail fractions compare the observed maximum silhouette and PC1 dip statistic with their reference distributions. We call this method "descriptive fitted-reference calibration." Missingness masks for the simulation are generated independently from the simulated values. In addition, selection across all model families is not repeated. A separated two-group positive control checks basic recovery. Neither this screen nor a projection-based modality test establishes clinical subtypes [Neville et al., 2026].
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.description: Independent Refitting, Consensus and Cluster Tendency
blocks.tested_text:
Twenty stochastic imputed data sets were created using bounded Bayesian posterior draws. Ten iterations of the chained-equations method were applied to each of the twenty imputed datasets. Separate k-means and sampled PAM methods were executed. Both methods were fitted with fixed k=2,3,4 after refitting domain scaling for each draw. For this ensemble method, PAM utilized two samples of 300 patients. Each of the cluster assignments contained exactly the same 1,457 validation patients. Agreement across draws was assessed using mean pairwise ARI and empirical 5th-95th percentiles. These percentiles are not confidence intervals since partition pairs share fits. A separate k-means discovery-silhouette analysis was executed to assess k=2,…,8 in each run.

Fifty 80% subsamples of discovery patients refitted preprocessing, imputation, scaling and fixed three-group k-means. A separate 50-run initialization experiment was conducted where the seed value for the clustering algorithm changed but the input remained constant. Patient sampling variability was evaluated by assessing the held-out ARI and matched per-cluster Jaccard metrics to distinguish it from initialization variability. Additional sensitivity checks evaluated mean and KNN imputations, no clipping, stricter test availability and independently fitted validation partitions.

Average-linkage co-assignment, greedy mean-NMI and generic NMF aggregation were compared as descriptive summaries of held-out assignment vectors, following [Tomo et al., 2026]. The native implementations are not an exact replication of that study. Consensus formed on validation assignments is not a separately validated predictive model. Collapsed groups and nonconvergence are reported.

blocks.tested_text: The new analyses identified repeatable groupings in cognitive test scores; however, their interpretation as distinct clinical phenotypes remains unresolved. The results shown below use the earliest eligible assessment for each of the 7,285 patients, comprising 5,828 discovery and 1,457 validation patients. They are not direct performance comparisons with the historical assessment-level UMAP analysis because the cohort, representation and validation design differ.

blocks.tested_text: The analyses were run using a version of Python (Python 3.12.14) that had all dependencies for each analysis at fixed versions, along with reproducible random seed settings, as well as the model grids specified above. A total of eight different numerical tests evaluated reference likelihoods, missing data recovery, EM algorithm monotonicity, preprocessing directionality, medoid selection, integrated trajectory likelihood, and the ensemble objective. No independent rehabilitation outcome is available, so predictive clinical utility remains untested.

blocks.tested_text: To be classified as a member of the longitudinal sample, an individual must have had at least three visits with seven or more observed tests and at least three distinct times. Additionally, there must be a span of 0.25-5 years between the first and last observation, and the patient's recorded age at injury must be consistent. Using the frozen index-discovery preprocessing, imputer and robust-space PC1 generates a longitudinal cognitive test score for each individual. This score is oriented toward better performance and divided by its index-discovery standard deviation. Finally, time is calculated as the number of years since the first time point when sufficient observation data were available. Regardless of whether an individual is a member of either the discovery cohort or the validation cohort, membership status will remain the same.

blocks.tested_text:
The results for representative solutions generated from the use of the discovery data are presented in Table 4.3. Two-group k-means and PAM were found to be preferable on the reference six-domain representation. Direct HDBSCAN assigned all observations to noise under both tested minimum cluster sizes. On the other hand, UMAP + HDBSCAN did produce classification into groups. Furthermore, changing the UMAP neighborhood size from 15 to 50 resulted in a changed group count and reduced measured-domain separation. Thus, this result suggests there is value in checking embedding-derived partitions in the measured features; however, it is possible to explore alternative parameterizations of density models.

K-means consistently identified two groups within each of the twenty stochastic imputations of the discovery-silhouette search. This is a consistent choice among k=2,…,8, not a test against one population. The eight-component full Gaussian domain model also reached the search limit. Neither silhouette-based selection nor a minimum BIC at the boundary identify a single, "natural" cluster count.

blocks.tested_text: The Gaussian linear trajectory mixture represents the integration of patients' random intercepts and slopes. One to four classes were fitted, with the covariance of random effects and the residual variance shared across classes. Each model used three initializations and up to 300 EM iterations. Discovery BIC selects only among converged models with sufficient expected membership in every class. Thus, if an estimated model does not converge or if the average probability of membership in a particular cluster is less than .05, the model is excluded from consideration. To provide a comparison point for our results, we have also included a single-class model as a continuous random-effects reference. Patient subsampling is conditional on selecting more than one class. Our focus was on examining observed patterns in this study rather than determining how much of the pattern is due to causality. The models do not implement nonlinear trajectories or the published multivariate contaminated longitudinal model. Recent longitudinal comparisons motivate separating initial level from rate of change [Julià et al., 2026].
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
Two- and three-group k-means were highly repeatable conditional on the robust-domain representation and bounded Bayesian imputation model (Table 4.4). Fixed three-group patient subsampling gave mean pairwise validation ARI 0.968. Varying clustering seeds with the input fixed gave ARI 1.000, and mean matched Jaccard values for the three groups were 0.994, 0.959 and 0.947. These measures describe repeatability within the specified pipeline; they do not establish that its groups are distinct clinical entities.

Average-linkage and greedy mean-NMI consensus agreement for k-means at k=2 and k=3 were similar. However, generic NMF aggregation was less reliable than the other two methods: in a two-group k-means ensemble, it reached its iteration limit and collapsed to one assigned group; the requested three-group version produced only two assigned groups. As such, this result concerns ensemble aggregation, not the historical NMF imputation method, and cannot be generalized across all NMF implementations.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
Robust scaling provided discovery variances of 7.93 for language, and 5.76 for orientation; those are larger than the 0.44 for memory. The first component explained 63.3% of robust-domain variance, however it loaded primarily on language and orientation. Narrow central ranges of ceiling-heavy scores amplify their tails under interquartile-range scaling. Equal-domain variance scaling resulted in the percentage explained by PC1 being lowered to 58.5%, and three-group validation assignments changed substantially: ARI between the two partitions was 0.243.

The silhouette value was 0.608 in the robust space and 0.440 in the equal-domain space, for the robust three-group labels. The silhouette values were 0.172 and 0.283 respectively, for each of the labels assigned to the three groups using equal-domain scaling. Figure 4.14 separates the partition effect from the measurement geometry. Neither type of geometric structure has been determined as accurate for use in medical applications. Using equal-domain scaling resulted in a decrease in mean agreement across imputations to 0.769 for two-group k-means and 0.747 for three-group k-means.

The robust solution contained three validation groups that included 1,221 patients, 185 patients and 51 patients. The smallest patient group showed a pronounced deficit in language skills, while equal-domain scaling provided patient groups containing 194 patients, 571 patients and 692 patients with different profile comparisons (Figure 4.15). As such, these exploratory profiles cannot be used as evidence to transfer the historical clinical tier names onto the new label designations.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
There are also relationships between test availability and the fixed three-group assignments. Cramér's V for cluster vs. missingness was .412 for MRAVLT075 and .371 for FEPMR. Missingness varied by group as follows: 10.2% to 80.4% for MRAVLT075, and 16.1% to 86.3% for FEPMR. These descriptive associations do not show that missingness causes the partition. They do, however, prevent interpreting repeatability under one imputation model as freedom from administration effects.

Fixed at k=3, mean imputation produced ARI of 0.921 compared to the reference grouping assignments, whereas K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) resulted in ARI of 0.538. If we restrict the sample to those who have had at least seven observed tests, then we retain 5,263 discovery and 1,339 validation patients and produce ARI of 0.903 on the common validation subsample. Eliminating clipping results in ARI of 0.958. Extending deterministic imputation to 50 iterations converged in 37 iterations, and did not result in any changes to the labeling (ARI = 1.000). Clustering the validation patients independently based upon the discovery transformation as "frozen" yielded an ARI of .895, which is an agreement statistic rather than another predictive performance metric.

Comparing raw-test aggregation with direction-aligned, standardized domain construction gave three-group ARI 0.703 over all assessments and 0.629 over complete cases. The attention composites were correlated -0.749 between constructions, indicating the impact of aligned directions and scales. These descriptive sensitivity analyses fix the completed values and represent no replication of the previously described supplementary multiple-imputation and complete-case analyses.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
Of the 32 incomplete-data mixture fits, 28 achieved a numerical convergence criterion. Table 4.5 provides the best BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) fit of those selected from each of the families, taking into account the minimum size requirement and the convergence requirement. The t-family with 4 degrees-of-freedom produced the best BIC and validation-likelihood of all the selected fits. Both t families selected eight components at the upper search limit, leaving the optimum unresolved. Their six-domain silhouettes were low. ICL also selected eight components for both t-families; however, it selected six rather than seven components for the contaminated Gaussian.

Therefore, these models improved the distributional-fit without producing eight validated clinical phenotypes. Many components may be used to simulate discrete score masses, skewness and tails. In addition, posterior-probabilities may be used to quantify membership uncertainty given the selected family of distributions and number of components, without considering either the uncertainty regarding which family to select or how the missing values arose.

In the 1,000-patient continuous-reference screen, the observed maximum k-means silhouette was 0.676, with a fitted-reference tail fraction of 0.0099. The PC1 dip-statistic tail fraction was 0.9901. The separated positive control recovered two groups with silhouette 0.917. These diagnostics provide different evidence: silhouette exceeds this particular copula reference, while the projection statistic does not show excess multimodality relative to it. These are descriptive reference comparisons, not an omnibus test establishing clinical phenotypes or excluding all continuous explanations.
blocks.review: Scientific meaning, numerical values, citations and qualifications reviewed; service errors corrected before the final detector check.

blocks.tested_text:
Trajectory eligibility retained 2,013 patients, with 1,590 in discovery and 423 in validation. All four fitted class counts converged. As additional classes were developed into the model, both the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and validation likelihood improved; however, every multi-class solution introduced a group below the 5% expected-membership threshold (Table 4.6). Therefore, the supplied selection rule retained one trajectory class with a continuous random effect representing each participant. Multi-class resampling was not triggered. Furthermore, it did not suggest that all participants recovered equally; rather, nonlinear patterns of continuous change, and small genuine subgroups remained unresolved.

This extension strengthens the evidence that reproducible partitions can be obtained in these cognitive scores. Its principal caution is that repeatability depends on representation and imputation assumptions. Scaling, missingness and distributional family materially affect assignments or component count. Ultimately, it is still uncertain whether distinct clinical phenotypes exist, or if they would have provided value given that there was no independent functional assessment.
